title: Ask, seek, knock (Matthew 7:7–11)
hookLine: what father gives a stone when asked for bread?
carry: ask, and it shall be given

cards: A kitchen, six in the evening. A small kid tugs on a parent's sleeve: I'm hungry, can I have some bread? The parent smiles, reaches into a drawer, and hands the child a rock.
Or the kid asks for fish and gets a snake. It's a horrible picture, and that's the point. Nobody listening on that hillside would do it.
The worst parent they knew wouldn't do it. Jesus uses that shock to say something about asking, and about who's listening when you ask.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." Three verbs, each a little stronger. Ask is words.
Seek is going out to look. Knock is standing at a closed door, making noise.
In Greek, all three are in a tense some readers hear as ongoing: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. Not one polite request and then silence, but a child who comes back to the sleeve.

Then the kitchen: "Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?" Some readers note that a small round loaf can look like a stone by the road, and a fish like a snake.
The fear under the question is real: what if I ask God for bread and get something that only looks like it?
Jesus answers with a how-much-more: "If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?"

Being evil is blunt: even flawed, ordinary people know how to feed their kids. God, he says, is not less kind than a tired parent at six in the evening. Christians are honest that this raises hard questions.

People ask for healing and a loved one still dies. Some Christians say the promise is good things, not everything, and that a wise parent sometimes says no or not yet. Others sit with the question unresolved.
What the passage clearly does is invite the asking. Plainly. More than once.

how: Christians often bring specific requests to God in daily prayer, returning to the same request over days or years, and some churches keep prayer lists so the asking is shared.

o: to demand what God owes you for your faith
to say a set prayer once, then let it go
to request plainly, and keep coming back again

games.q: the three verbs and the kitchen — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus pairs a fish with a snake as well as bread with a stone
"Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent?"
Jesus compares God to ordinary, flawed parents
"If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more."
Christians all agree every request is granted
some say the promise is good things, not everything; others leave the question open.

games.q: you're a parent at six in the evening. your child asks for bread. what do you hand over?
games.why: that's his point. nobody hands a hungry child a rock, and God, he says, is not less kind than you.

practice: Think of something you actually need right now, not the polished version, the real one, and say it in the simplest words you can, the way a child would: I need help with this.
If you pray, you can ask God for it, just like that; if you don't, notice what it's like simply to name the need out loud. Then sit.

wordCard.voice: Ask. The first of three verbs: ask, seek, knock. Some hear in the Greek: keep asking.

orig.note: Greek: ask! a present-tense command, which some hear as keep asking.

carryVoice: Your line: ask, and it shall be given. Bread, not a stone. That's two hundred fifty-six.
